profile.reading: This is The Deck, a data center in Tampere, Finland, originally developed under the Ficolo brand and later operated by Verne (formerly Verne Global) before being sold, along with sister facility The Rock in Pori, to Nordic cloud infrastructure provider Glesys in a deal announced October 14, 2025 on undisclosed terms. The Deck offers up to 1 megawatt of power capacity across about 400 square meters of technical space, considerably smaller than its underground sister site. Verne stated the sale would let it concentrate on its own expansion plans, including a planned 70 megawatt facility in Mantsala and growth of its Helsinki campus, describing the move as part of a long term strategy focused on AI ready colocation across the Nordic region. Glesys, founded in 1999 and acquired by Cube Infrastructure Managers in 2023, already operated data centers in Falkenberg and Stockholm, Sweden, and Oulu, Finland, and had previously acquired Moment Digitals Finnish data center business in Tampere, making this Ficolo owned Deck facility a further consolidation of its Finnish footprint. Before the Glesys sale, Ficolo Oy had operated three Finnish sites, Helsinki (the Air), Pori (the Rock), and this Tampere facility (the Deck), all powered by 100 percent sustainable energy, and began operating under the Verne Global brand starting October 18, 2022, when the two companies combined to form a broader Nordic data center platform with about 23 megawatts of available capacity and potential to expand to 90 megawatts across the three Finnish sites. Both Verne Global and Ficolo were, at the time of that combination, part of Triple Points Digital 9 Infrastructure plc portfolio, and Verne separately operates a renewable powered campus in Iceland that was expected to reach 40 megawatts of constructed capacity in 2023, plus a data center hub in London.

reading.body:
The Deck, a 1-megawatt data center in Tampere, Finland, changed hands from Verne to Glesys in October 2025, part of a broader consolidation of Nordic AI-ready infrastructure powered by renewable energy.

The facility represents the modular undersized end of the data center market. At 1 megawatt across 400 square meters, it is considerably smaller than its sister site The Rock in Pori, yet it operates at full capacity in a region where power availability constrains growth. The sale to Glesys, which already held Ficolo's other Finnish assets and the Moment Digitals facility in Tampere, indicates consolidation of fragmented regional capacity under a single operator.

The transaction occurred as Verne pursued a focused expansion strategy around a planned 70-megawatt facility in Mantsala and growth in Helsinki. This suggests that smaller legacy facilities no longer aligned with Verne's scaling objectives, even though The Deck and The Rock had been marketed as part of a unified Nordic platform with ambitions to reach 90 megawatts across three Finnish sites. Glesys, backed by infrastructure fund Cube, appears positioned to operate the portfolio at a lower growth rate, absorbing available capacity without requiring the new megawatt-scale builds.

The data does not cover utilization rates, customer composition, or whether the sale indicates weakness in the Nordic data center market or simply asset reallocation among operators with different capital strategies. It confirms only that renewable-powered capacity of this scale continues to trade hands as AI infrastructure buildout concentrates around larger facilities and specific geographic nodes.
